Without all guarantees.) 4th Year. Berlin, Tuesday, December 1937 By Haßell Became the German battleship "Deutches Land" in print. Rome, December 27. The admiral of Haßell departed on Monday accompanied by the naval attaché, Captain Commandant Lange, aboard the battleship "Deutches Land," which was anchored in Naples after Christmas and New Year. Admiral Mareschal gave an early report from board, including the admiral of Haßell, the general councilor and naval attaché along with their wives, as well as the commander of the admiral of the lower Tyrrhenian Sea, Admiral Valli, his wife. A grandson of Mussolini was born in Rome on December 27. The wife of Vittorio Mussolini, the oldest son of Italy's prime minister, was discharged from the hospital on Monday by a boy named Guido, who is to be born in Turin. Italian studies commission departs for Tokyo. News of the upcoming dispatch of an Italian studies commission to Japan receives lively support in the Italian press. The director of the "Giornale d'Italia" explains that political, patriotic, and cultural cooperation, fostered and deepened by both sides' efforts, is a necessity when one considers that the two countries have equal positions and problems. Italy and Japan are today together with Germany in the defense struggle against communism, the greatest threat to the cultural world. The responsible politics of Rome, Berlin, and Tokyo rests on the resolved will of their governments and peoples, which relies on a strong military and follows a clear goal through which no one is threatened. Nevertheless, no trace of the hostile sentiment directed against the three powers can be observed yet. Thus, at this very moment, American pressure once again turns against Japanese naval activities at sea, although these did not come close to the American construction programs in the distant past. The equality, which is allegedly one of the foundations of democracy, will nevertheless be vigorously contested on the area of naval disputes as well as on other vital areas by the three great imperialist and warlike democratic powers. Against the advance of the great self-interest and privileges, however, a separate defense was offered. A military formation of foreign legations. Vienna, December 27. The legations have recently not only strengthened their agitation but are also trying to expand their organization. What is new is the founding of an "Eisenische Legion," which primarily consists of young people and aims to perform order and protection duties at gatherings. Formerly voluntary military formations were dissolved in September 1936, with the fatherland's front granting it sole rights, in agreement with the federal army, to establish and maintain armed formations. Memelites honored by the Lithuanian state president. Kowno, December 27. The Lithuanian state president has pardoned the ten convicted men sentenced to ten years in prison by the war court in the Neumann's Saßmann proceeding: Kwanka, Grau, Kuhn, Riegel and Lapins. New blow against the churches in Soviet Russia. Moscow, December 27. According to reports from Moscow, the GPU has found a new means of inflicting death on the few churches still not closed in the Soviet Union. After that, a regulation appeared stating that starting January 1, 1938, taxes, with which churches and chapels are leased, will be increased by 120 rubles. It cannot be doubted that the churches will not be able to pay these taxes; according to the decree, the smallest remaining church in Moscow is expected to pay 25,000 rubles this year. It appears there is also the opinion of the GPU regarding the enormous expense, which may force the Christian communities to close the churches. Sweden's hospitality demands trade agreements with France. Stockholm, December 27. The main organizations of the Swedish hospitality have written to the foreign ministry requesting the re-establishment of trade relations with national Spain. In the letter, it is stated that immediate measures must be taken to negotiate an agreement on concluding a trade and shipping treaty with national Spain. Only such an agreement can allow Sweden to fulfill its interests on the Spanish market. Heavy displeasure from the Bolsheviks in Teruel. San Sebastián, December 27. As reported by the army report from Sunday, the heroic resistance of the national Spanish troops in the city of Teruel continues. The Bolshevik hordes were subjected to heavy displeasure. The national troops continued to reinforce their positions. Two red aircraft were shot down. Armed Bolshevik attacks at Teruel. Bilbao, December 27. Even on Monday, the 12th day of the Bolshevik attack, the battles in Teruel continued. The national air forces bombarded enemy positions on the city's outskirts and conducted follow-up operations. They inflicted great displeasure on the Bolshevik attacks on the fortress of Teruel, which were primarily carried out by foreigners. Although the Bolsheviks are resisting the national troops advancing toward their liberation with their best forces, they must retreat slowly. The national troops under General Aranda have already succeeded in capturing some important heights. On both sides, new doubts arise constantly. The head of the general staff of the national Spanish hospitals thanked the nurses in Teruel in a call and urged them to continue their efforts. The commander of the 1st army corps expressed hope in a radio message that the high soldierly virtues and the heroic struggle of the city of Teruel will soon lead to decisive success. German participants on the star flight to the Sahara under the command of Mühlig, his deputy Dr. Mülberger, and their deputy Leutnant von Harnier, who are each on board a 240 PS motorboat for the star flight to the Sahara organized by the French Aero Club and the Algerian Aero Club, arrived at Le Bourget airport in Paris around 4 p.m. on Monday. The German aircraft will depart from Le Bourget on December 29 and proceed over Bordeaux — Biarritz — Nimes — Paris — Rome — Naples — Palermo — Catania — Tunis to Algiers. They departed Sunday the route Rangsdorf — Breslau — Stolp — Berlin and on Monday the route Berlin — Cologne — Paris. The third German aircraft has not yet been transported to Berlin and will depart next Monday with the NSFK group Lufthanäta, flight captain Klitzsch and radio operator Schnurr, in order to reach as many of the other two aircraft in Algiers as possible.

Paris, 15th February. Efforts seem to be underway in France to allow the French parliamentary elections to take place following the German federal elections. From the government's side, it has been repeatedly assured that the elections are scheduled for April 22. Yesterday evening, rumors suddenly emerged during the chamber's proceedings, reporting a shift in the election date.

Paris, 15th February. As reported from Casablanca, the unrest in the area not yet under French control has intensified so much that the French military administration has decided to dispatch an expeditionary force. A bombardment of the Beaulieu region is planned, where former residents of General Governor Steeg were stationed. To achieve more effective success in the bombardment, a new recruitment center for numerous mountain dwellers has been chosen.

"Paris, 15th February. The impeachment chamber yesterday rejected the motions of Blumenstein, Laeze, and Simon Tovbini on provisional release."

Berlin, 15th February. The Berlin Daily News reports from Wiesbaden that an appeal against the integration plan of Frankfurt am Main has been filed by the Rhineland Commission.

Saarbrücken, 14th February. The French mining directors have already begun mass evacuations of miners with a shift-based pay system. At the "Velsen" mine, workers aged between 54 and 62 were dismissed without notice. There are even reports of a suspension of this mine.

Butarest, 14th February. The National Farmers' Party has reached an agreement with the Socialist Party for a joint struggle against the government.

London, 14th February. According to reports from New York, American Admiral Plunkeii has stepped down from his position as fleet station commander in Vancouver after giving a speech at a dinner where he reiterated his earlier statement that war is unavoidable according to his view. Plunke added, however, with a softening tone, that there is still a risk nearby.

General Strike Aftermath.
Post Service of the Zurich Students (Correspondence). The post dispatch by students during the general strike in the city of Zurich was undoubtedly one of the most pleasant images amidst the gloomy, serious days we endured. How friendlier, warmer, and more dutiful this cheerful, duty-bound young team was in the atmosphere of bitterness and hatred, encouragement and terrorism. As order and discipline failed, as post workers, instead of fulfilling their duties, were dictated to by political schemers and turbulent chatterers, it was the academic youth spontaneously stepping forward out of a desire to be useful and serve the general public that offered itself to the post and telegraph walling. Initially, its goal was to bring the demands for resuming work back to the striking personnel. Then came the dispatch of letters, packages, and telegrams. Strict regulations regarding the secrecy of postal matters did not allow it to proceed further without further involvement from the hundreds of students who had joined the main post on several hundred hands. Each one had to be formally employed as a post messenger first by announcing the federal criminal code articles and then hired as a post office attendant. And what was even more difficult, for each of these dispatch orders, a military escort of 1–2 men, along with many classmates, had to be provided to ensure sufficient protection against threats and incidents from the striking side. This precaution proved unfortunately unnecessary. Individual students were actually attacked by Bolshevik agents on the street or in private residences during the dispatch tour, and if no harmful consequences arose, then this should be considered luck. In the outside world, a dispatch group accompanied by four soldiers was seized at a village hall and threatened.

But despite these dangers, our students were not deterred. With fire and skill, they dispatched their letters and then worked quickly from one door to another, from one apartment to another, greeted with joyful welcome by the bourgeois population everywhere. To avoid the insults used by strikers, they did not care for the profane words that were shouted at them. They knew what lay ahead: the welfare and independence of our country, the suppression of the quiet, willing working population by a terrorist minority. This fresh aggression, this boldness, this grasping of the seriousness of the situation by the academic youth gives us hope as well to look forward into the future. Our people will not compromise its rightful path if its best sons lead from true patriotism. And Zurich's academic youth crowned their activity with a waiver of compensation offered for service to demonstrators. They transferred nearly 2000 francs, approximately in November, to the collection fund in favor of the Zurich soldiers shot dead by the Lucerne soldiers who served as messengers! Basel. In the restoration of order and peace, in Basel, the military and police will be supported vigorously by the citizens. This organization has already seen about 6,000 citizens from all ranks join. Less exemplary was the stance of the executive council regarding the strike. Only when the actual state strike was announced and larger unrest loomed, did it finally decide to seek military aid. On that day, the government even went so far as to negotiate with the strike committee for a written guarantee to maintain peace. Fortunately, it did not happen. When the news arrived on Thursday morning that the Olten action committee had unconditionally capitulated, it refrained from addressing the federal council regarding the requested withdrawal of troops. If the executive council, with its admirable conduct, indeed pursued the admirable intention of securing a peaceful outcome for the strike, then it must have been considered a weakness.

In the Grand Council meeting on November 14, sharp criticism was also directed at the executive council's stance. It was thrown back that it had failed to fulfill its duty to ensure peace and order, and in fact had even been willing to hand over its power to strike leadership. During the government presidency of Dr. A. Im Hof (lib.), and the executive councils of Dr. Aemmer (freis.) and Dr. Miescher (lib.), A. Stöcklin (freis.), Dr. Mangold (wild), E. Wullschleger (soz.) and Dr. Hauser (soz.) took a contrary position. The unconditional disapproval of the majority of the government's stance toward the population has now led to its resignation, by which executive council A. Stöcklin submitted his dismissal request to the Grand Council.

With all rigor, the authorities were brought to trial against the instigators of the strike. All speakers from all bourgeois factions stood on their side decisively. The speakers of all civil factions spoke unanimously in favor of the execution of cheaper reforms.

Baden, November 20. The council of Baden, headed by National Council member Jäger, published its latest session announcement: During the recent revolutionary state strike, unfortunately, urban workers were also endangered by treason against the municipality through treachery toward the community. In accordance with Article 352 O.R., all contributions to the city and municipal works are now open for public use, so that any act of service refusal will result in dismissal. The municipality has requested that the "Free Aargauer," who shamelessly propagate revolutionary propaganda, be denied official publications by the municipality until further notice. If there is constant opposition, the demand is made to prohibit the publication "Publication organ of the municipality of Baden" from appearing in the subtitle of the "Free Aargauer" (Social democratic daily newspaper of the Canton of Aargau).

Neuchâtel. The balance of the recent general strike days is not difficult to draw; it concludes with a factual defeat for the organizers of this movement. In the districts of Reuenburg, Boudry, Val-de-Travers and Val-de-Ruz, where thousands of workers are employed in various industrial sectors, nothing was struck. For Locle and La Chaux-de-Fonds, the same would have happened if not the electrical power line had been broken, which the socialist administrations of these two places, intentionally or otherwise, were unable to restore.

What surprised those who listened most from the Olten action committee was the hard-nosed resistance of the strike opponents. Everywhere, citizen militias were immediately formed, and the large number of Newburger youth stood on the side of order and freedom friends. The executive council issued a proclamation in which it invited the population to take up arms against the social disorganization that the general strike means. This appeal had its effect. The government received lasting and effective support from the Newburger people, who maintained their silence and cold-bloodedness. Already since Tuesday evening, November 12, fatigue was observable among the strikers, as a precursor to capitulation, which was announced on Thursday throughout the country.

Our social democrats had to endure the bitter reality that brutal complicity would have no success. In the face of impending danger, these social defense organizations, which were just formed, will remain, and it is not doubtful that another strike or uprising attempt would have less success than the one that so sadly failed just then. The steadfast supporters, who claimed that they had moved further to the far left in recent years, were unanimously approved of. The disciplined workers, whose union banners they carried, participated in the patriotic demonstration on Thursday evening in the main city with great enthusiasm.

Against the socialist authorities of Locle and La Chaux-de-Fonds, responsible for the power outage, even in the hospitals, a general storm of resistance is directed. They would be removed if elections were taking place now. On the other hand, the cantonal authorities are unanimously approved due to their calm energy, which allowed peace and order without military intervention to prevail.

The awakening of patriotism among the struggling youth was particularly noted. Without doubt, from now on, theories of the far left in these circles, in which a shift to the left was observed in recent years, are condemned to failure. The striking railway workers do not forgive their breach of duty, and thus accept it no less than they should have received fair wages and large price increases. They demand that they be exemplarily punished so that they can see the magnitude of their error, which already endangers the already difficult state means of living even more.

In one word, the success of citizens and authorities fighting the general strike is a complete success. As in the time of the 50-year anniversary celebration of the Republic in 1898, the Newburger people fulfilled their duty, and with justified pride today they see that its Swiss patriotism still exists in full strength. The Benjamin of the Confederation is better than his name. He has proven it in these difficult times of examination. Our Swiss comrades may think about this when we will push for more democracy and greater respect for the rights of the people in Bern.

Love Gifts for the Military. For the landstorm company stationed in Rapperswil, a collection was organized by the civil side, which yielded 4324 francs. From this amount, each of the 180 landstorm soldiers received a conscript's pay of 20 francs. The remaining amount will be allocated to the currently still 26 field hospital caretakers, who housed 9 soldiers at the emergency hospital in Rapperswil.

The Bündner Gebirgstruppen 92 and 93 are pleased with their warm welcome by the population, which greeted the teams through donations of fruit (over 15,000 kg.), tea, cigarettes, etc., generously. Unfortunately, under these troops is also suffering from the flu, fortunately, the cases are almost less severe.

The Bündner government has agreed to provide a special military allowance of 2 francs per day to each volunteer offered for the fighting week, as a token of gratitude and recognition for their loyal service.

Church Lottery in Schifflingen

Rising Production Rate in West Germany  
Frankfurt am Main, August 27 (AP). The economic situation of the Bi-Zone is making rapid progress, explained yesterday by the director of J.E.I.A., W. John Logan. The production rate has increased significantly over the past two months and now stands at 60 percent of its level in 1937. Two factors responsible for the beginning of the economic upswing are the currency reform carried out in June and the efforts of J.E.I.A. to stimulate imports and exports. Imports into the Bi-Zone amounted to $282,400,000 in the first seven months of this year, which is more than in the entire previous year. Brigadier M. R. L. Robinson, a staff member of Logan, told press representatives that plans to consolidate the economy of the French Zone will be advanced. On questions, he said there have been no unexpected difficulties here. He reminded them that the unification of economic administrations between the British and American-controlled double zone even took several months after this decision was made. As the likely date for joining the economy of the French Zone, he named the beginning of next year. Logan then clarified false representations related to J.E.I.A., which appeared in various newspapers from the Soviet-licensed "Berliner Zeitung" to the American "Wall Street Journal." Regarding the claim by the "Berliner Zeitung" that J.E.I.A. has put the Bi-Zone into a "forced jacket" to benefit the United States, Logan said:

"All revenues from Bi-Zone exports were used for imports. Moreover, the United States will spend about one billion dollars on life-saving imports to Germany. How can one speak of profits for America in this regard?"

Clarification by the French Military Government on the Borsig Demolition in Berlin  
August 27 (AP). Due to inaccurate and deliberately misleading press reports about "looting" of the Rheinmetall Borsig factories in Berlin since the French occupation forces — the reports were published in the Soviet-licensed press — the French military government issued the following clarification:

1. Before the French authorities took over their sector in Berlin, most of the machine park, meaning around 2,000 machines, was already independently dismantled and transported by Soviet occupation forces.
2. Before the liquidation of weapons material, the Rheinmetall Borsig factories were referred to as a weapons plant by representatives from the Soviet Union, England, and France on June 15, 1947. This decision was confirmed by the Coordination Committee on July 29, 1947.
3. In fulfillment of this resolution, the responsible Soviet, American, British, and French authorities declared the Borsig factories as reparations facilities.
4. According to the provisions of the aforementioned resolution, the inter-allied Repair Aid Authority in Brussels (IARA) allocated equipment for this operation to a number of member states of the United Nations. The electrical power plant was excluded from this list by request from France.

The majority of the machines were supplied to Western and Eastern Europe by the states at their request, especially Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia. France received only 100 out of the 1,800 machines.

Wien, Samstag, den 1. Juli 1911. Wien, 30. Juni. Die glorreiche Erinnerung an die Wiener Stichwahl wird in den heutigen Beschlüssen des Deutschen Nationalverbands mit keinem Wort berührt. Nochiges Schweigen für die großartige Kundgebung einer deutschen Stadt mit zwei Millionen Einwohnern; kein Zeichen der Herzlichkeit und kein freundlicher Gruß für eine Bewegung, aus der auch für die nationale Politik ganz neue Werte gekommen sind. Kann dieses Nebenwesen der Deutschen in Wien und in den Kronländern nützlich sein; muss der Deutsche Nationalverband nicht als wichtiges Ziel erkennen, die starken, werbenden Kräfte der alten Kaiserstadt, wo jeder Stein von der deutschen Geschichte erzählt, für seine Politik zu gewinnen; würde nicht der Augenblick, da die politische Zukunft wieder unsicher geworden ist, besonders dringend, die Beziehungen zwischen Wien und dem Nationalverband natürlicher und wärmer gestalten? Die älteren Parlamentarier, die dem Sturmwind des allgemeinen Stimmrechts nicht weggeschleudert hat, mögen sich noch immer erinnern, dass in den Anfängen des Grafen Taaffe eine Versammlung in den Sophiensaal einberufen wurde. Dort hat Franz Schmeykal, der Führer der Deutschen in Böhmen, der deutschen Stadt Wien beide Hände entgegengestreckt. Wer die Wirkung erlebt und sieht hat sie niemals vergessen. Auf der Tribünestand: Franz Schmeykal, damals in Wien persönlich noch wenig bekannt. Er begann zu sprechen, und schon nach wenigen Minuten waren alle Blicke voll Spannung auf den feinen Kopf mit den leuchtenden Augen geheftet, und jeder Satz, jede Geste wurde von den Hörern unterstrichen. Wien, das sich die Politik so gerne in einer Person versinnlicht, schloss ein Bündnis mit Böhmen und mit allen Deutschen in Österreich. Wäre dieses Beispiel, das Franz Schmeykal gegeben hat, nicht auch jetzt nachteilig, und sollten nicht die verantwortlichen Träger der deutschen Politik in Österreich eine Brücke schlagen zwischen Wien und der parlamentarischen Vertretung vom deutschen Volk? Die heimlichen Ursachen des letzten Ministerwechsels werden bald zu spüren sein. Das halbamtliche Kommuniqué über die neue Orientierung der Politik sagt dem Erfahrenen genug und vermehrt das Bedürfnis, die Bürgschaften und die Wälle, die das Schicksal der Deutschen in Österreich sichern können, zu verstärken. Deshalb darf Wien weder vernachlässigt noch zur Seite geschoben werden. Hier lebt ein Fünftel aller Deutschen in Österreich und ein noch viel größerer Teil aller freisinnigen Deutschen. Eine Politik, die sich umschlossene Fundstellen des nationalen Gedankens nicht kümmern wollte oder dagegen gleichgültig bliebe, wäre geradezu unzulässig. Wien hat zehn freisinnige Abgeordnete gewählt. Davon mögen zwei und vielleicht drei wegen ihrer scharf ausgesprochenen besonderen Richtung und wegen älterer Verständnisse für den Deutschen Nationalverband nicht in der heutigen Nummer enthalten sein: "Landwirtschaftliche Zeitung": "Neues auf dem Gebiete der Zuckerfabrikation." Vom k. k. Regierungsrat A. Stift. Seite 25 bis 27. "Militärisches Nachrichtenblatt" der "Neuen Freien Presse": Aus dem Landwehr-Verordnungsblatt. Miszellen. Seite 28. Weiter: Die 64. Fortsetzung des Romans "Frühlingstaumel" von Gabriele Reuter. Seite 24. Feuilleton. Alfred v. Berger und seine "hamburgische Dramaturgie". Von Otto Ernst Louis Schneider, der Vorleser Kaiser Wilhelms I., soll einmal nachgewiesen haben, daß die Berliner Zeitungen seit dem Jahr 1768 alljährlich mit großer Einigkeit versichert haben, so weit wie gegenwärtig das Theater noch nie herunter gewesen ist. Es mag jawohl Dienstboten geben, die ihre Schuldigkeit nur dann angeben, wenn sie unaufhörlich gescholten werden (obwohl ich an die Zweckmäßigkeit dieser Pädagogik nicht recht glaube), und in Deutschland scheint man das Theater für solch einen Dienstboten zu halten. Siebenmal in jeder Woche hat das Theater, sowohl in Hinsicht des Repertoires als auch in der Betrachtung des Theaters. Dann bleiben immer noch sieben, vondenen jedoch nur zwei zu der für nächsten Freitag einbeziehenden Versammlung des Deutschen Nationalverbands eingeladen wurden. Diese Beschränkung mag in der Form durchaus zu rechtfertigen sein, weil bisher nur zwei Abgeordnete erklärt haben, dass sich sieben Deutsche Nationalverbände anschließen wollen. Es braucht auch nichts in diesem Beschlusse gewittert zu werden, was den Verdacht begründet könnte, als sollten gerade solche Mitglieder des Parlaments vom Nationalverband ferngehalten werden, von denen die Christlich-Sozialen in den Wahlen niedergerungen wurden. Abersehen die strengste Korrektheit wird die Frage nicht erhellen, ob dem Deutschen Nationalverbande selbst nach sieben Stimmen noch wertsein können. Es hat im früheren Abgeordnetenhausemanche Kämpfe und Krisen gegeben, in denen der Deutsche Nationalverband um jede einzelne Stimme zitterte und die Grenzscheide zwischen Mehrheit und Minderheit auch von sieben Abgeordneten gezogen werden konnte. Der Deutsche Nationalverband kann überhaupt kein Mandatentbehren, das von deutschen und freisinnigen Wählern herrührt. Gewiss werden diese sieben Abgeordneten von Wien niemals dem deutschen Volk in den Rückenfallen und auf die heißesten Schlachtfeldern als Freiwillige sich zur Verfügung stellen. Die Führer des Deutschen Nationalverbands wissen, dass sie innerlich darauf rechnen dürfen. Wäre es nicht kleinlich, dies diesen sieben Abgeordneten alle Pflichten des Nationalgefühls aufzuerlegen und ihnen die Rechte zu verweigern und davon mindestens nicht anzubieten? Ein freisinniger Abgeordneter von Wien kann nur deutsch sein, und der Nationalverband sollte ihn daher durch einen Beschluss, der ihn zu einer Bitte um Aufnahme zwingt und vielleicht sogar einer Demütigung aussetzt, nicht gewaltsam zum Freischärlermachen. Das heißt, auf die Hilfsquellen verzichten, die Wien für das deutsche Volk hat; das heißt, die Deutschen in Wien und Nichtwiener trennen; das heißt, einen Fehler begehen, durch den eine große Zukunft preisgekommen wäre. Die politische Verschmelzung von Wien mit den Kronländern muss das Ziel des Deutschen Nationalverbands sein. Er kann diese zwei Millionen vom deutschen Besitzstande, den er sonst mit aller Wachsamkeit verteidigt, nicht wegstreichen. Er sollte Wien gefürchtlich erobern und nicht von sich stoßen. Der Beschluss des Deutschen Nationalverbands, nur zwei Wiener Abgeordnete zur konstituierenden Versammlung für nächsten Freitag einzuladen, mag in der Form durchaus zulässig gewesen sein. Es handelt sich jedoch nicht um das strenge Recht, sondern um jenes politische Gefühl, das mehr ist als Klugheit, weil darin die Gabesteckt, die Wähler anzuziehen; auch weil sich darin tiefere Einsicht und schärfere Voraussicht zeigt. Eine milde Auslegung hätte leicht finden können, daß diese sieben Abgeordneten sich meistens als deutsch und fortschrittlich bezeichnet haben und somit im politischen Zusammenhang zu einem Tiefstand erreicht, der nicht mehr zu unterbieten ist. Es kann übrigens sein, dass diese Erscheinung nicht nur in der Beurteilung des Theaters auftritt. Ich habe die Beobachtung gemacht, dass die Leute über einem Regentag sieben Tage Sonnenschein vergessen und daß sie, wenn es gar drei Tage nacheinander regnet, auch nach einem guten Sommerversichern, ein so elender Sommer wie dieser nicht dagewesen ist. Es gehört viel Courage dazu, solchen Schimpfmoden zu widersprechen; aber in diesem Punkt bin ich dreist. Wir haben eine Operettenpest und haben Laboratorien für ihre Verbreitung, das ist mir bewusst; wir haben auch sonst eine dramatische Schundliteratur und Theater genug, die ihr dienen; aber alles in allem haben wir auch eine große Anzahl ernsthafter Theater, die ein vortreffliches Repertoire vorführen, und im Durchschnitt steht das Theater heute mindestens so hoch, wahrscheinlich aber erheblich höher, als es oft gestanden hat. Ich hege den Verdacht, dass ich zu dieser günstigen Meinung gekommen bin, weil ich die Dinge verstehe, und will gleich erklären, was mich in diesem Verdachte bestärkt hat. Vor kurzem sagte mir ein namhafter, auch von mir selbst sonst aufrichtig hochgeschätzter Schriftsteller: "Seitdem ich das Theater aus eigener Beobachtung kenne, kann ich nicht mehr darüber schreiben; ich habe meine besten Dinge über Theater geschrieben, als ich nicht die Spur Davon verstand." (Ich weiß, lieber Leser: Oskar Wilde pflegte der gleichen Sätze als sehr begreiflich und wohl begründet zu vertreten, ich weiß, ich weiß.)

text:
France.
Paris, July 3rd. Indeed, no time has been more inventive in spreading rumors than when nearly every week journals publish false reports for publication, because the same public opinion excites them. If one wanted to investigate and refute all rumors that explode like mushrooms from the ground without wanting to provide an account of their origin, it would be a task as arduous as ungrateful. We are only fulfilling our duty to warn the German public that our conditions are indeed too dark and that already stormy weather is on the horizon, whose breach is near. What can one say from the state of affairs that Count Orlov has stayed here longer than we initially thought, and who knew our political informants that the extended presence of the Count, introduced into the most secret intentions of his sovereign, signifies a firm protection and loyalty bond between France and Russia, whose foundations are already established. We give this count no greater importance than he deserves. It is simply because of the fact that our cabinet in some political questions sympathizes with the Petersburg Cabinet. That from this leads to an even more elementary agreement is beyond question. Even about our internal affairs and matters, every day brings new rumors, which spread like lightning from mouth to mouth, although the press has no right to notice them. All things forbidden excite public curiosity; what cannot be said here escapes attention, and finds itself increasingly prominent in London and Brussels newspapers, where it appears on an ever-larger scale, and precisely that effort by our rulers to make the foreign press serveable contributes to this belief that people are trying to hide things from the public, so as not to have to illuminate them. If our press were only half-free, one would not believe the absurd statements, which the faithful souls will find enough. Do not worry some about a second Fructidor in the attics because the Orleans do not deny their sympathies, because the Nepublians, despite the recent outbreak of news, are willing to reconsider and present their candidates when called upon for the upcoming elections? Even the latest state councilors still have a large public audience, because the government has not yet decided on the same measures, and so it is no wonder that our political atmosphere weighs heavily on us as the Senegambian heat, under which we sigh all week. (D.)

From the Western Front

The Battle of Noyon.
The correspondent from the Neutertor reports to the French Army that on June 10 at 2 p.m., after midnight: The battle continued throughout the night and morning. Noyon is still in our hands, while the Germans managed to breach our line in the center by throwing new troops into our ranks. They advanced southwestward toward Eauigny and Thiocourt. The fighting was extremely bloody. This time there were no surprises for us, because during the last 36 hours before the start of the battle, our troops had been exposed to heavy artillery fire. We must expect a longer and more intense fight. Terrain losses should not discourage us: The Daily Telegraph correspondent at the Western Front reports that the Germans may know from their mouth which mouth has taken no special precautions for what kind of new attack plans they have. For days we observed troop movements, doubling "the transportation of all kinds onto the advance routes in the current offensive area," and an extraordinary increase in artillery activity, reformation of batteries, and so on. There were unmistakable signs of the Germans' intention to attack Montdidier's advance. The French artillery fire was relentless; the cannons knew the terrain very well.

French Commentary.

Regarding the advance from the line of Montdidier-Noyon, French newspapers express themselves according to a report by the Agence. Hannes is confident that this offensive has reached its peak. The military employee of the "Journal" claims that the Germans have already taken so far as their 190 divisions, which they allegedly possess: since the beginning of the major offensive in the west, so far in advance that their "weariness and fatigue need will very soon become apparent," Mati can say from experience that even the largest offensive cannot be sustained for more than three and a half months. The "Journal des Temps" is of the opinion that the actual goal of the Germans was achieved and this goal has not been reached. The situation on the plain of Montdidier certainly did not improve, but it also did not change. The "Temps" writes: It is undeniable that we have retreated, but the favorable reaction we exercised in the center of the battlefield speaks for itself regarding the determination and bravery of our troops. We must trust that our supreme command allows the enemy to expend his forces in very costly attacks in order to expect only distant exhaustion with a deployment of reserves and with an expectation of success.

Despite the improvement in our line, Gustav Herve writes, there is still uncertainty. The great fear that there is power in military circles underestimating the tide moving through the Marnelands cannot be denied. It is beyond question. We have been under the influence of a German storm surge since March 31 from the imagined attack on Calais and Amiens, and we have repeatedly said and repeated in the press based on assurances from so-called secretly supported circles that it could very well happen that this specter has taken root in the minds of our great leaders, and that there is no fear left to hold the French back. Paris is not a point like any other. It is a point where at least one tenth of our population lives. Moreover, Paris is our most powerful industrial center; it is the largest concentration of wealth in Europe—it is the center and hub of France: Herbe writes that the French divisions did not hesitate to cover all threats as they seemed threatened, and that publicly no shame is being held for the French. Paris can be covered by English divisions whenever necessary.

American Troop Reports.

Reuter reports from Washington:
War Minister Baker stated in a speech to the French Alpine Rangers that more than 700,000 American soldiers are being sent to France.

France, Paris. The National has issued the following words to the ministers: "No, no, it does not count on our ignorance; if you want an uprising, then you will not have any of them. What we want today is a demonstration whose calm will terrify you and proclaim the will of an entire population. We want that with the deputies,
with the voters, the officers, the soldiers of the National Guard, with all citizens who still hold onto their sense of right; we want to prove to you that your arbitrary impulses have a peaceful, unarmed and unoppressed mass against themselves, whose all-powerful voice will suffice to show you what respect you enjoy. Order will make our strength. The capital of ideas will set itself in opposition to you and remind you of the loose determined by counter-revolution. The people of Paris need no battle;
they know that it is enough for them to show themselves to defeat you."

Neaples. The constitution signed by the king and ministers on February 10, published the next day consists of 89 articles. In the preamble, the king calls God a witness to the purity of his intentions and the firm resolve to remain loyal to the new political order. It is well known that the new constitution is based on a two-chamber system, in which the royal sanction is required for every law. The initiative belongs equally to the king as to the chambers. Among the general provisions, we highlight that the equality of citizens before the law is proclaimed and that individual freedom guarantees the inviolability of private property, even literary property, the right to private residence and letter secrecy, the right to petition, press freedom, and complete judicial independence are ensured. In ecclesiastical matters, however, strict intolerance prevails; only Catholic worship can be practiced, further, writings dealing with religious subjects are subject to censorship. For the Swiss, Article 10 reads: "No foreign troops can be taken into service of the state without a law (which is naturally the province of the chambers); the existing conventions should, however, be respected." No laws, not even municipal regulations, can be raised without the consent of the chambers. The direct provisions are voted on annually; the indirect ones can take several years. The budget is a matter of the chambers. The chambers appoint an accounting chamber, which takes insight from state accounts. No property of the state can be sold without the enactment of a law. The National Guard must be introduced. Its education and composition will be determined by a law; only it is established that elections for officers shall be held by the national guard itself. This appears to us as the most essential provision among the general regulations. Then follow three sections on the chambers. The relationship between the chambers and each other, and again with the king, is like in France. The king is chosen from among himself for life; he has, however, voting rights stipulated in the constitution. Ten clergy are allowed. The number of members is not fixed. Deputies shall be elected on a one-man vote of 40,000 citizens. Both voting and election are subject to a census; its determination is reserved for an election law that is yet to be enacted. The professors of the royal university, members of the Bourbon academy, municipal officials, the military, etc., are eligible voters. All non-removable officials cannot be deputies.
The fourth chapter deals with the person of the king, who is sanctified and inviolably declared in other constitutions.

Regarding the appointment of a regency upon the death of the king (if he has not determined anything about it before his death) or
when the same is physically impossible, taking command,
the chambers take part; they designate two or more princes of the royal family, who form the regency with the queen. Chapter 5 describes the ministers.
The deputy chamber can also put itself into a state of suspension, whereupon it will be governed by two or more princes of the royal family, chosen from among themselves and subject to the judgment of the deputy chamber. The king may pardon the condemned ministers only if an explicit request is made by one of the chambers.
A law should determine the details thereof. A state marshal of 25 members elected by the king gives advice on the affairs assigned to him. Also here, a law should determine the details. In Chapter: Courts, who...

Germany. Prussia. Berlin. In Charlottenburg, there were clashes between the Prussia Association and the democratic association of Schläger. According to correspondence from the Fr. O. P. Z., the Prussia Association used a venue that the democratic association utilized for its meetings and demanded its vacating. From word exchanges, a serious dispute arose. The Democrats largely fled to avoid being struck by the "Prussia," while others escaped into stables, and some even into chimneys. During the flight, one so recklessly shouted "Republic" on the street that he was beaten down. The injuries sustained are so severe that it is doubtful of the individual's return. The republican Edgar Bauer is also severely injured. This correspondent reports, among other things, that in the aftermath of these events, Berlin itself became agitated. A large number of workers mobilized. However, this ultimately ended with the arrest of 10 leaders of the workers. On Unter den Linden, however, notable groups remained gathered, circling the square to approach Charlottenburg. The report continues without further details.

No 49. Provincial - Correspondence. December 6, 1876. The 24-year-old. Before the latest resolutions on the judicial system. The Reichstag has reached its highest possible task in a short period of time, which allowed all the faithful the serious collection for the final concluding acts. The great laws, which should establish legal unity among the German people, are now fully examined in the second, factually detailed lesson, and it is expected that the final lesson will follow within about three days, in which it will be discussed how to finally resolve the remaining opinions that remain unresolved on the danger of the inevitable failure of the massive work. If one considers the entire course thus far, the magnitude of the common dedication of all who participated in the work and those who gathered together for it—the result achieved so far—so little is it possible to believe the failure of this work: no one can take responsibility for such a failure without the deepest, indispensable grounds. In this sense, the federal governments are most certainly taking another look at the great reform project, as outlined in the second reading of the Reichstag. What was said in the second lesson—that the wishes presented to the Reichstag before the beginning of the second lesson, which were not given the hoped-for consideration due to a series of fundamentally important points—will once again be examined with careful consideration of the views held and opinions expressed in the Reichstag—to determine how compatible or unavoidable it is for the final work, according to their conviction about the final outcome, to accept responsibility for the welfare of the people. It should not be forgotten that the governments did not believe they could fully assess what is insufficient for the German people alone—yet with full respect for the convictions of the majority of the Reichstag and with all willingness to consider them—they can help institutions that they themselves consider inherently harmful to the national goal achieve its national objective. That is why it is expected, even more, that the Reichstag will once again carefully reconsider the final resolution on the matter of justice and the rights of the people. From multiple statements in the second lesson, it was to be understood that the majority considered themselves obligated, at all important questions, first and foremost by their own convictions and fundamental demands of the constitution—political party standpoint point of view—to lay greater influence on the legislative process. Of this standpoint alone should be taken into account: the large number of votes with which individual proposals presented in opposition to the resolutions submitted by the governments were expressed does not necessarily constitute an absolute obstacle to a final resolution; because these votes, which opposed individual questions of government opinion, will now, according to the resolution itself, impose greater influence on some of those questions of duty for the collective agreement. From this standpoint alone should be taken into account the large number of votes with which individual proposals presented in opposition to the resolutions submitted by the governments were expressed—not as an absolute hindrance to a final resolution.

Certainly longing eyes now turn towards a certain goal in the lands of Germany, one that they have never left their minds with sharper attention, and those concerned individuals secretly shake hands and believe in the signs of time for their work a favorable constellation to find them. They greeted the change (as they call it) in Prussia with jubilation the system's change (which they name) entering now into the liberalizing regime that is approaching. The Nine Elms, which until then remained quietly and sagely beneath the earth surface were now vigorously digging themselves out since such encouraging liberal rains on the dry Prussian land have never been so eagerly sought after. They work and labor with power; they process and are election voters and all already are a movement in Berlin, as it has not been for 1848 anymore. What do certain people say loudly, which only faintly recall the finest first revolutions of then? And where else?
Incorrectly assured legitimate public organs and sensible people have never experienced a system change in Prussia, but merely a personnel change; that certain people are not willing to continue their work, and it is even stated that it would now have been no system change but merely a personnel change? What matters now is that certain people do not insult us; they give themselves at most the word: "For now, retreat!" We have already moved a good distance closer to the goals; for the voters are inflamed, the hopeful-hearted voters intensified their efforts. The "new era" in Prussia.
They will be dissatisfied with this new negation if they do not fulfill their wishes; furthermore, when taking advantage of this liberal opportunity, they have learned from their people how to do so; it has become clear that one can build right time for these and those here; they have once again sown an artful portopenny weed among the weeds. — What is this doing? — Certain people are not harmed; they give themselves at most the word: "For now, retreat!" We have already moved a good distance closer to the goals; because the voters are inflamed, the hopeful-hearted voters intensified their efforts.
The "new era" in Prussia will be dissatisfied if it does not fulfill its wishes; moreover, when taking advantage of this liberal opportunity, they have learned from their people how to do so; it has become clear that one can build right time for these and those here; they have once again sown an artful portopenny weed among the weeds. — What is this doing? It clearly runs a red thread through this appearance, and anyone can see it; except for those who feel comfortable in it, it can be dreamed of with certainty.
But that awakening will likely not wait very long and is after God's own time not to look at the reeds. No one, however, conceals itself that all over Germany under the surface discreetly stirs, and no one gives themselves to foolish hopes; there is no enemy because no one sees him. Radical liberties cannot die, but the radical spirit does not die; it has only become more cautious since 1849 and is now truly aware where it can act.
The Swiss have paid their time for this delusion;
they were after the victories of the Sonderbund in 1844 and 1845 entirely delighted and reassured, they dreamed of a long-time vanquished enemy; alone this enemy recognized his time; in 1847, under the encouragement and wishes of certain liberalizing countries—which then had to endure enough suffering—he rose with full brutality; the noble cantons bled in this principle struggle and came into radical servitude; the liberal neighbors celebrated; it showed itself in the German west with the first swallows of revolution; in Baden a preliminary parliament was held, one printed "the people's wishes" was ready, which then became "Förde"; and it had only needed February 1848 and the unleashed flood to break free and spread unchecked all sides. It is precisely this red thread that must not be left out of sight, carefully followed, and not let oneself deceive when it suddenly conceals itself somewhere between a white-black or white-yellow surface.
(M.)

I have lived in good and happy circumstances, and no motive has ever been able to bring me away from this reserve. The Emperor added that I could fully understand the firm character of the Crown Prince to know that nothing is harder than shaking his conclusions or moving him to abandon a once accepted system, and that he, the Emperor, is convinced that it has before us an attack on Copenhagen. As the English ministry assured the English nation that the Emperor did not express even the slightest displeasure over the raid into Shetland at the beginning, there will be no interest in reading any further explanation regarding a conversation that took place between the Emperor of Russia and General Hutchinson prior to our attack on Copenhagen. The Emperor added: — so reports General Hutchinson — this conversation is weighed with the question of what I think of our attack on Copenhagen? I replied that the circumstances which might have led to such an action were entirely unknown to me, yet I hope that the English administration will justify itself and that the whole world can prove that the Danes were in the process of uniting their entire power with the French against England. The Emperor noted that I could not possibly entertain this idea if I had still considered the uncertainties we had in Bartenstein. In these, the Emperor said to me that he has used all possible means to enable the Danish Crown Prince to enter into the coalition against France; that but the answer of the Prince was always clearly and unalterably the same—that he had maintained neutrality for many years—so firmly resolved his own government; that his people were thus found in a Dane-Danish government. I said, I believed that Lord Gower had sent the Emperor's ministry a note on this subject, upon which the Emperor confirmed that it was so, yet the content of the note is laughable, as such notes contain no genuine information. The Emperor spoke near about the great distress caused to you by our unanswered attack, and that nothing similar has ever happened; that if such an event were to occur, all circumstances that have previously determined the relations between nations would take place, and that in the case of any thing, anyone could do what he pleased. The Emperor said to me in the most certain expressions, with the firmest tone, that he had enough for this, without taking all the provocation at all, attack; that this is his duty as Emperor of Russia, and that he has enough. He asked me if I dared to speak on this subject again, as he said further; that the most feeble treaties and obligations bind him with Denmark, and that he was determined to fulfill such obligations. The Emperor added: — he suspects we are thinking of an attack on Kronstadt; that he cannot foresee the outcome of such an attack, but will continue to resist until the last man stands, and that in the event of this happening, everyone who can do it is entitled. I replied that I had every reason to protest and believe that we would not attack Kronstadt. He answered that he had done so, and his decision was unwavering. After that, he ended the conversation, and repeated with great emphasis: "That he wants sufficiency for Denmark" — the Freemason of April 7th contains the following:
The Hamburg correspondent says, from Petersburg, and in the latest Berlin newspaper, that H. von Rotberg died in Ehstland. There are many reasons to doubt the authenticity of this notice; it is curious, moreover, how hastily such unvarnished notes are sent to the public, which would be deeply shaken by them! The Emperor's ministry also mentions on April 22nd at the great parade at Peterburg that Swedish flags and a flag sent by General Burhöyden were seized.

In brief from Paris on August 3rd states: "An ordinance has thus spoken for the dismissal of H. de Vitrolles as State Minister. So this man, who comes from lower folk classes (he is the grandson of a guestmaster in the Alps), Secretary of State for the Ministers' Affairs, State Minister and member of the king's private council, gathered 80,000 francs together, gradually losing all his posts and incomes; and all these sacrifices he has given to intrigue himself!" He is given as the author of the letter addressed to the foreign sovereign, which French people sent to move them to interfere in our domestic affairs. In this letter, the question is discussed very seriously whether the hostile ministry can save France? They decided that it was not capable and requested the powers to put themselves at the disposal of the King of France for a minister more favorable to the tastes of H. de Vitrolles. — His secretary, H. Lasitte, is in custody; hope is that his explanations, and the interrogation which H. de Vitrolles himself unquestionably will undergo, will finally draw out the authors of that letter into dim light and teach us what class of French people must resign themselves to public disinterest. The service of H. de Vitrolles has aroused a harsh reaction from the friends of the king and their country. With pleasure, it is maintained how the government developed a strength necessary for maintaining peace. A new course of action by the state represents the line they have drawn themselves. It troubled H. Agier, substitutes of the royal guard at the Parisian court, his position; for some time he has been on the side of the throne's enemies, and he had him suspected of being one of the agents of the last conspiracy. This young man, full of reckless self-interest, believed himself to be determined to great things; since it failed him, leaving him in a subordinate position within the ministry, he formed himself into a means that would allow him to strike back if he were to take against his sovereign. From this course of action one can infer his tactics and judgment. — The wife of Herzenberg, Princess of Brunswick-Bevern, has arrived in Paris to marry her niece, Lady von St. Augur, with the police minister. The leader of the ultra-royalists seems to be equally drawn into the hand of H. de Casteljean. They are very aware of the brilliance spread by this connection over him; they are very aware of the new evidence of trust and respect with which the king honors him; and they will rush over the discovery of the conspiracy, which increases the regard and fame of a minister who sacrifices his health to protect himself from becoming enemies, so that he may perform ever more daily services to his sovereign."

France. The two proposed railways, heading towards Orleans and the Havre, are expected to experience little impact within the chambers' offices. Only regarding the privilege against competition is there a differing view.

As reported in the Journal du Hayre: "We learn that a ship's surgeon has given his correspondent in Havre the order to send several crates from our port to England, so that they can depart there—whether in Bristol or London—with the first steamship scheduled to set sail for New York. Since international attention is now focused on the new connection opening between England and America, there is no cause for concern that Switzerland and northern Germany will allow the crates previously sent via Havre to take their place through London or Liverpool?

Under a somewhat peculiar name—a health insurance company—has formed a society in Bordeau, which has earned applause and imitation everywhere where people believe in improving the condition of the poor for a cause. The society is: to cover all expenses incurred by its members each week from 40 cents per person, who could be affected by their own illnesses; to provide them with a daily monetary allowance of one franc during their illness if they pass away; and finally, to secure those who become unable to work due to age weakness or misfortune through an annual pension of 100, 200, or 300 francs, depending on whether they have been members for 10, 20, or 30 years. Those eligible for a pension of 300 francs may choose instead a position in the hospice that the society is establishing for this purpose (2nd A. 3.)

(The Times). It is assured that the Duke of Angoulême is very ill; his loyalists are very distressed about it; we speak here of the rational, because according to their view, the Duke plays the role of moderation and knows how to restrain excesses or delay them; and they ensure that if this rumor once disappears, the young Duke of Bordeaux would like to be subjected to harmful whispers and the heat of his character.

Hannover. A heated debate in the second chamber is said to have caused a protest from the peasantry of the Electorate of Osnabrück, which now circulates in frequent copies. The election agents explain that only the example of other revolutions moves them to choose one; but they do not at all acknowledge the validity of abolishing the state constitution.

The second chamber is currently more than 20 members stronger than before the holidays, and many new representatives are expected this week between Holy Week and Pentecost. The Hanoverian newspaper contradicts news that the commission of the German federal parliament, which has been proposed as a mediator for the Osnabrück petition, should explain itself competently. The commission has not yet issued any report, assures the Hanoverian newspaper. If that news had only expressed the commission's intention, it could at least be true.

Rom, May 24. Professor Gervinus is here from Göttingen. He will spend some time here to use Rome's libraries for his studies (A. Z.)

From the Italian border, May 20. The Cologne annals are hoped to be concluded peacefully. So much did the papal chair feel offended by the removal of the archbishop that it determined on his reinstatement into the Cologne episcopal see before he could enter negotiations with the Prussian government; so it seems he was indeed motivated not to express this demand at all, but that even without that condition helping to resolve the disputed issue, he depends equally on removing that question. To this end, the head of the general vicar of the Cologne diocese, Dr. Hüsen, has allowed the leadership of the archbishopric in the absence of the archbishop as its representative and to handle it. (A. Z.)

Belgium. The mayor of Tilff, Mr. Neef, was elected deputy from Liège; his opponent, Mr. de Longrée, who was supported by the clergy party, and a close relative of the minister, Mr. de Theux, fell through. The election was contested fiercely because Mr. Neef had 445 votes and Mr. de Longrée 413.

Turkey. The establishment of quarantine stations must alienate the rightly-minded Turks, who never believe in contagion because they only become ill if God wills it. The Turkish state newspaper takes it upon itself to justify the new station even in the spirit of the Prophet, and one may assume that its article was not written without a remnant of conscience-angst. Here are some of the most curious passages: "It is known to everyone, and the theological and legal books teach that God has the power to create and destroy all things in the world without any cause. Only we find in the Quran and in the oral traditions of the Prophet that the highest essence possesses great wisdom and mercy, and that it creates and destroys through causes. Accordingly, it is necessary that in order to quell hunger, one must eat, to soothe thirst, to drive out disease, to take medicine, and above all to return to the causes and means. Some theologians insist unconditionally on trusting God; only then can one take the necessary measures and still trust God. Moreover, the ability to take such measures, as well as the effectiveness of these last remedies, is possible only through the grace and permission of the Most High."

Dresden, May 26. The authorized representatives of the Zollverein states to be found at this station have arrived. In Darmstadt, Dr. Fr. Heldmann, once employed as a teacher in Aarau and Bern, died; he was also known in Swiss journalism as the editor of the European newspaper published in Bern. A work on Freemasonry appeared in Aarau in 1819.
